newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl allies seek balanced budgets, tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Kohl allies seek balanced budgets, tax cuts.

text.p: Germany's Free Democrats (FDP), Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition partners, approved a neo-liberal reform programme on Saturday demanding constitutional changes to ensure balanced budgets and low taxes.

An overwhelming majority of delegates at a party congress approved the "Wiesbaden Principles", the culmination of moves by the FDP over the past few years to focus on free market economic values such as privatisation and deregulation.

The programme calls for changes in the German constitution to oblige all levels of public administration to achieve balanced budgets within 10 years and set an upper limit on the tax burden of an average citizen.
"The new FDP is a reform party fighting for more freedom and responsibility for the individual," general secretary Guido Westerwelle told around 660 members of the liberal party.

Westerwelle said the FDP, which provides Kohl with his 12-seat parliamentary majority, would use the programme in a drive to become Germany's third party -- the traditional postwar status which it has lost to the environmentalist Greens.
"We want to reconquer third place in the party structure with distinctive policies. Simply helping another party to gain a majority is too little to be worth fighting for," he said.
Opinion polls show the FDP hovering around the five percent barrier a party must overcome to be represented in parliament.
The programme also calls for a constitutional change to require a two-thirds majority in the national parliament or in state assemblies for the introduction of any new tax.
Westerwelle said the way to cut Germany's unemployment total of more than four million was to roll back the frontiers of the state to give more reponsibility to private enterprise.
Pointless regulations were stifling the formation of new businesses and frustrating a new generation of young entrepreneurs in the mould of Microsoft founder Bill Gates, Westerwelle said.
"Bill Gates wouldn't have been possible in Germany," he said. "He began his business in a garage -- and a garage doesn't have a window and two seperate toilets."

Westerwelle said the FDP, which has styled itself as the champion of lower taxes within Kohl's coalition, would continue this line despite looming budget shortfalls for 1997 and 1998, when general elections are due.

"The subject of tax is a question of freedom for us," he said. "When more than every second deutschemark is passing through the hands of the state, that means there is too little of the market economy, not too much."

The programme concentrates largely on economics but also includes measures dear to the party's civil liberties wing, which used to form its maintstream, such as giving more rights to foreigners living in Germany.
